events.excerpt: The highest priorities for the transition to post-quantum cryptography are the basic building blocks of authenticated key-agreement protocols such as TLS. Without these building blocks in place, secure communication on the Internet will not be possible once cryptographically relevant quantum computers come online. However, today we rely on quantum-vulnerable cryptography for much more than TLS. Privacy Pass is a protocol used by site operators like Cloudflare to help protect applications from abuse. One way we do this is by rate limiting individual clients so that no one client consumes too many of the site's resources. Normally this involves some combination of friction or loss of privacy for users: CAPTCHAs or other challenges to moderate traffic, along with accounts and fingerprinting to identify traffic.Privacy Pass was designed to avoid this tradeoff between friction and privacy. The basic idea is that a client gets issued a number of tokens , which they can redeem in exchange for access to the site. Crucially, each token is unlinkable to the client it was issued to, ensuring the client can use the site as they always had without sacrificing privacy. events.excerpt: Daniil Ankushin, Nethermind. Verify-budget figures: method by Daniil Ankushin, benchmark and measurements by Manuel Arto. On frame transactions a shielded pool pays its own gas, so a private withdrawal needs no relayer. We ran a real BN254 Groth16 pool this way on current Nethermind master: a withdrawal costs 679,322 gas. With EIP-8250 nonce keys, many withdrawals can come from the one pool address at once. Two things do not work yet. The proof check is over the spec cap on validation gas, and a pool cannot pay for a call from the user’s own address. The pool we ran is soispoke’s minimal-shielded-pool ( GitHub - soispoke/minimal-shielded-pool · GitHub ). How a withdrawal works In a withdrawal the pool is the sender. Its VERIFY code checks the zk proof and approves execution and payment. The user needs no funded account and does not appear in the transaction. Two drafts make this safe in a public mempool. With EIP-8250 the pool uses the note’s nullifiers as nonce keys. Each withdrawal has its own nonce key, so withdrawals with the pool as sender do not compete for one nonce. A side effect: a nullifier that was already used is a used nonce key, so the protocol refuses a double spend before the pool’s code runs. events.excerpt: Last week’s security notice on the Fearless Wallet browser extension ( notice ) says that from February 2025, unlocking the wallet sent your private key to a server run by the attacker. The notice links a write-up that walks through the code at fixed commits ( write-up ). I read it and then went through the repo history myself. None of it was hidden. It sat in public source the whole time. I audit smart contracts, not browser extensions, but the review lessons carry over to any code that touches keys. Like the write-up, I’m sticking to what the code and the history show, not who wrote it or why. How it got in, and how it left The code arrived in PR #1022 of soramitsu/fearless-wallet-web, titled “Ton Service”. It was open for ten weeks and merged on 19 February 2025 as one squashed commit, “TON ecosystem”: 251 files, 4,690 lines added and 6,119 removed. The PR has no review comments. The function that matters is about 25 lines, in a new 180 line file, inside a diff of almost 11,000 changed lines whose title says it adds TON. It left the same way. The code was deleted from the source on 25 June 2026, inside a release commit with about 80,000 changed lines. What each piece looked like in a diff The name. events.excerpt: Last week at GitHub Universe, we announced our new Git storage architecture, capable of handling thousands of writes per second with reads that scale on demand. Through internal testing, we’ve demonstrated the ability to support 5,000 concurrent agents working on a repository, sending 7,200 pushes per second to a repo, all while serving read traffic with consistently low latency. This new architecture is the foundation for GitHub to support agentic development for hundreds of millions of developers, and we’ve been building it underneath GitHub while it keeps running. Over the past year, agents changed what a busy repository looks like on GitHub. In our first post in this series, we laid out the two principles behind our next-generation Git storage architecture: minimize coordination, and decouple storage from compute. In our last post , we covered the bridge: moving 99.99999% of repositories into Azure, scoping the write quorum to individual references, and standing up virtual replicas backed by Azure Blob Storage. We also left off with an observation: very little of a write needs to be ordered. Git objects are immutable and named by their contents, meaning two writers can store them at the same time without agreeing on anything. The part of a push that needs agreement is the ref
events.headline: Inside GitHub’s new Git storage architecture

events.excerpt: AI Agents now act on the web for millions of people. To a Site, an Agent can take many forms. It may be indistinguishable from a human user carrying out a task, or it might look like one visitor carrying many Users. This removes the ability for the Site to recognize, serve, and hold accountable the user or users behind the Agent, and causes the Site to face the costs when something goes wrong. This post argues that in order for Sites to maximize the access they provide to Agents, the ecosystem must develop new mechanisms to preserve the relationship between Sites and Users. Traditionally, in Security and Fraud Prevention, that requires three things: Identity, Reputation, and Accountability, allowing Sites to answer: Is the person acting being truthful about who they are? Is that person trustworthy? And who answers for the action? “Personal AI Agents” (“Agents” for short) are automations that take instructions from a human (“User”) and pursue a goal by controlling a cloud computer or browser. They are usually hosted and maintained by an “Operator” as part of a managed service or consumer offering. Examples include Muse from Meta and dots from OpenAI, and more are launching all the time. events.excerpt: Hi all. We recently opened a discussion in the Solana SIMD repository about a new class of smart contracts we’re loosely calling “inference programs,” or “Actually Smart Contracts.” We’d value technical input from this community on whether a similar proposal could be feasible on Ethereum, before we write anything for it. The idea, briefly: a contract stores a prompt and the rules that shape it (a DAO constitution, a policy, a standard). Another contract asks it a question with evidence. AI models from different operators answer off chain, each signs a vote, and the caller checks the signed result before acting. The motivator was Anthropic’s recent work on zero-knowledge proofs of LLM inference . The Solana drafts and the discussion so far: Overview and drafts: Bringing Inference Programs To Solana Microsite with diagrams and a sandbox: asc.verafy.ai Discussion: solana-improvement-documents #724 We have no strong view on whether this is technically feasible, and we know there is a lot of prior work here that we may not have accounted for, including optimistic oracles and opML. The drafts were written with help from AI tools, so some of it may be poorly reasoned. The questions we’d most like help with: Is this better as an application-level ERC, or not a standard at all? events.excerpt: Walraswap: equilibrium-based decentralized exchange integrating external AMM liquidity This is an announcement of the research article with the same title and a brief informal intro for ethresear.ch. A classic approach to tackling MEV in decentralized exchanges on Ethereum is to enable a mechanism that receives trade orders during a block interval and settles all the swaps in a batch following a fairness criterion. It is an old problem. I imagine that an informed reader might feel somewhat skeptical. Thoughts of this kind were expressed in 2014 in this Reddit post . CoW Swap, UniswapX, 1inch’s Fusion, Sorella’s Angstrom, and Propellerheads’ Turbine have all tackled the problem using batch trading in one way or another. Walraswap started in 2023 at Flashbots, independently of the previous and closely related work by Ramseyer, Goyal, Goel, and Mazières: Augmenting Batch Exchanges… and SPEEDEX . The central feature in common: we treat the DEX problem from the point of view of the theory of equilibrium for an exchange economy with n tokens. To understand equilibrium in two sentences: given a finite set of trade orders, under mild hypotheses and neglecting transaction costs, there exists a price vector —an equilibrium — at which all the orders can be executed with no deficit or surplu
events.headline: Walraswap: equilibrium-based decentralized exchange integrating external AMM liquidity

events.excerpt: Accessibility work often lives in issue trackers, contribution guidelines, audit reports, team knowledge, and conversations with users. When that information has no predictable home, people who encounter a barrier must search for it, and maintainers lose context as contributors and project ownership change. An ACCESSIBILITY.md file, now visible on repository overview pages, gives a project one durable place to explain its accessibility goals, contributor expectations, supported environments, known limitations, and process for reporting barriers. GitHub makes accessibility statements easier to find GitHub now recognizes the ACCESSIBILITY.md file in the repository’s root, .github/ directory, or docs/ directory. events.excerpt: Abstract This standard defines a proxy that coordinates execution sessions by temporarily caching a program and its associated calldata in transient storage. The proxy forwards the cached program to a fixed implementation through DELEGATECALL and uses a handler flag to control whether subsequent reentrant invocations are dispatched. The program remains unchanged throughout an execution session, while the cached calldata is replaced on each accepted invocation. This enables a single implementation to coordinate callback-driven execution using different programs and calldata without deploying a new contract for each execution. Motivation Many advanced execution strategies require dynamically changing execution logic, particularly when interacting with external contracts that invoke callbacks during execution. Traditionally, dynamically changing the execution logic of a contract may require deploying a new contract containing the desired runtime code. This introduces deployment costs, including contract creation and code-deposit costs. Flash Loan Proxy separates the execution program from the implementation responsible for interpreting it. Instead of deploying a new contract for each program, callers provide the program as calldata. The proxy temporarily caches the program and forwa

events.excerpt: Proposal Type : Ratification Executive Summary This Ratification vote adds an Upgrade Authority Transfer policy to the Governing Policies section of the Standard Rollup Charter. It sets out how a Chain Governor may request that upgrade authority for its chain be transferred from the Security Council to an address of its choosing, so the chain can manage upgrades itself or through a third party. Under the policy, the Optimism Foundation confirms a valid request and publishes a public notice on the Governance Forum. After a mandatory 30-day notice period, the Security Council is directed to execute the transfer. Once the transfer is executed, the chain ceases to be a Standard Rollup. This is a non-fork upgrade. It changes Charter language only: no smart contract or node software changes are required, and this proposal executes no onchain transactions. Motivation The Standard Rollup Charter defines how a chain becomes a Standard Rollup, including authorizing the Security Council to perform upgrades. It does not define how a chain leaves. Today, a Chain Governor that wants to take back upgrade authority has no published path, and any transfer would require ad hoc governance action. events.excerpt: Release Notes Node version 11.2.0 is a pre-release version of cardano-node that is not yet recommended for use on mainnet. Its headline change is the move to the new cardano-config library for reading node configuration: the node now understands a versioned configuration "envelope" alongside the existing flat format, and the configuration files published for each network are now in the envelope format. It also extends the gRPC interface, continues the groundwork for the Dijkstra era, Leios and Peras, and fixes several operator-facing bugs. Highlights: New configuration format. Configurations are read through cardano-config . Existing flat configurations still work. The new envelope format ( $schema / Version / MinNodeVersion / Configuration ) is schema-validated. New cardano-node config migrate , cardano-node config schema and cardano-node config resolve subcommands convert, describe and check a configuration. The shipped network configs are now enveloped and cannot be read by nodes older than 11.2 . gRPC over HTTP/2. The gRPC server can now listen on a TCP address/port, in plaintext (h2c) or with TLS ( --grpc-listen-address / --grpc-listen-port , --grpc-tls-* ), instead of only a unix socket. New gRPC methods ReadMempool , WatchMempool and ReadEraSummary , plus server reflection

Abstract Deploying and distributing private smart contracts, confidential L2/Validium state diffs, or permissioned intent payloads across Ethereum’s public P2P and Data Availability (DA) layers currently faces a fundamental metadata bottleneck. Even when contract bytecode or state is symmetrically encrypted, existing Broadcast Encryption (BE) and Attribute-Based Encryption (ABE) schemes require attaching an explicit cleartext header specifying either the authorized recipient indices, covering subsets, or the target access tree. In this post, we propose an architectural framework based on Stealth Attribute-Based Broadcast Encryption (Stealth ABBE) over BLS12-381 ( Zenodo Preprint ) for zero-metadata delivery of private contracts and encrypted state on Ethereum. By reformulating broadcast access control as a homomorphic blind Reed–Solomon decoding problem over 𝔽 256 using carry-free Base-3 packing in exponential ElGamal ciphertexts (𝔾 1 × 𝔾 1 ), Stealth ABBE achieves: O(1) Broadcast KEM Size (24.1 KiB amortized): Fits comfortably inside a single EIP-4844 blob (~19% of one 128 KiB blob) regardless of the total participant count N . Zero Visible Headers or Revocation Lists (0 Bytes): Access policies, cohort rosters, and revocation states are algebraically absorbed into the non-system
events.headline: Stealth ABBE over BLS12-381: Zero-Metadata Broadcast of Private Contracts & Encrypted State via EIP-4844 Blobs

events.excerpt: Executive summary Ethereum’s upcoming enshrined Proposer-Builder Separation (ePBS) introduces new ways for validators to participate in block-building markets. Most importantly, it enables builders to compete directly for block proposals, with payments guaranteed by the Ethereum protocol, reducing the need for trusted intermediaries. This proposal seeks to preserve the principles of Lido’s existing MEV Policy while adapting it to ePBS: maximizing rewards for stakers, supporting open and competitive block-building markets, and ensuring that Node Operators (NOs) do not favor particular builders or withhold MEV rewards. Following the discussion in Lido’s call for an updated MEV policy . It proposes a two-track approach: 1. An open, permissionless market where Lido validators can accept bids from any builder meeting Ethereum’s protocol requirements, provided payments are guaranteed by the protocol. 2. A vetted market where builders and intermediaries offering additional payments outside Ethereum’s guarantees must be approved through Lido’s Allowed List. Both tracks apply regardless of how a bid arrives: via p2p, a direct connection, or through one of the available sidecars. events.excerpt: Personal agents are the intermediary between humans and the Internet, turning a person’s instructions into requests and actions on websites. A customer might ask a personal agent to compare products across your site, find support articles, or complete a purchase. To a site owner, all three interactions show up as automated traffic — and without a clear view of which agents are visiting and what they are doing, it can be difficult to know whether that traffic is helping your business or creating risk. Blocking agents altogether can feel like the safest choice, but it can mean losing customers. Better visibility into agent activity allows you to decide what access makes sense for your site. Today, we’re launching new analytics to help you understand how personal agents access your site on behalf of humans, along with more granular access policies to put those decisions into practice. Together, they let you welcome agents on your own terms, and in ways that support your business. See how agents access your site Knowing which agent is behind a request turns unexplained automated traffic into traffic you can act on with confidence. Cloudflare maintains the largest verified bot directory in the world, and we are now bringing that intelligence into your traffic details. In Security Anal

events.excerpt: Status: a design proposal for discussion. Nothing in this post is decided. Changes described here would need to go through governance with token holders’ approval. Dates are aims, not commitments. 1. Context Two complementary developments were proposed that could affect validators in the near future. The first is the move to Metanodes, described in a forum post by Adrian . Besides relay chain consensus, validators would take on node roles that the ecosystem currently funds separately, starting with collation and full nodes for Asset Hub and People Chain, potentially with further roles such as Bulletin Chain as opt-in. Over time, this could replace the separately funded RPC, collator and bootnode setups. For validators, it would mean more work per node and stronger hardware. The hardware requirements are published in the Polkadot docs. The second is a smaller active set. A forum post by Jan-Jan proposes reducing it step by step via three referenda, one week apart (600 → 500 → 400 → 320), with the aim of completing the reduction before the end of 2026. The first referendum has already been submitted. Each step would require Fellowship whitelisting and a token holder vote. Together, these developments call for recalibrating validator rewards. Validators who take on more work and run
events.headline: Proposal to Recalibrate Validator Rewards for a Smaller Set and the Move to Metanodes

events.excerpt: Hello, I’ve opened a PR for a new opcode, SLOTDURATION . It pushes the duration of the current slot, in milliseconds, onto the stack. PR: Add EIP: SLOTDURATION Opcode by Amxx · Pull Request #12619 · ethereum/EIPs · GitHub Open questions: Current duration or historical lookup? The draft returns the current duration. The Rationale describes an alternative where the opcode takes a slot number and returns the duration in effect at that slot, or 0 for future slots. That would let contracts like Lido’s compute correct timestamps across duration changes. The cost is that the execution layer would have to keep the duration schedule. Which is more useful? Milliseconds. I chose ms to match SLOT_DURATION_MS and to support L2s with 100–250 ms block times. Any objections? 0 for “no regular interval.” Is this the right sentinel for on-demand chains, and should L1 execution clients still reject 0 ? Execution-layer decoupling. EIP-8198 deliberately keeps the execution layer unaware of the slot duration. The draft keeps the EL config-free, but it does add a header field. Is that acceptable to the EIP-8198 authors and to client teams? 3 posts - 3 participants Read full topic
events.headline: EIP-8484: SLOTDURATION Opcode

events.excerpt: Protocol This release introduces protocol version 39 On mainnet , this protocol version can be enabled no earlier than 2026-11-05 07:42 UTC (start of epoch 549). Please ensure that you update your validators before this epoch change. Otherwise, if the upgrade threshold is reached, the protocol will remove you from the committee, and both you and your delegators will lose rewards. #13131 : From protocol version 39 on devnet and testnet, random beacon DKG that misses its timeout round keeps running and can enable randomness again mid-epoch instead of disabling it for the rest of the epoch. #13169 : Protocol version 39 enables consensus_dedup_only_recorded_messages on all chains. A consensus message is skipped as a duplicate only of an earlier message with the same key that was recorded as processed or, in the same commit, passed verification, so all validators reach the same decision about a later copy of a dropped message. #13300 : Raise the minimum validator joining stake to 6M IOTA, the low stake threshold to 5.5M IOTA and the very low stake threshold to 5M IOTA. #13285 : From protocol version 39, a multisig whose committee mixes Ed25519 with other key schemes is only accepted when every committee member has signed. #13308 : groth16::prepare_verifying_key and groth16::verify_gro
